document_title: Alaska AI Contracts and the Comma That Hides One
post_copy:
Search federal contracts for artificial intelligence among Alaska vendors and you get 24 records or 25 but never both.

Zero records in common. One contract ends September 10th, 2026. Leisnoi Professional Services, $20,632,119.41 obligated, 8(a) sole source.

It began September 11th, 2025. Koniag IT Systems ended the day before. The Kodiak linked line runs back to 2019. The Joint Artificial Intelligence Center is on it. Now it is the Deputy to the Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office. The names changed. The sentence didn't. All of it is lawful.

Four contract numbers with their totals, and the two search results that don't share a single record.

What string should a citizen have to type to see all seven years at once?

#AlaskaAI #FederalContracts #ANCSA

aftercare: Post Tuesday through Thursday between 8 a.m. and 11 a.m. Alaska time, and get this one out before September 10th, 2026 (C11), because the whole close rests on a date that is days away and a passed deadline reads as old news.
Paste the sources comment within about 60 seconds of posting, straight from the block above and unedited, so every raw FPDS query URL survives the paste unbroken.
Open the post on a phone once the comment is live and confirm each query link is tappable and that none of the long FPDS URLs wrapped into the label above it.
Stay on the post for the first 60 to 90 minutes and answer every comment with a claim id, a number or a query string, never a thank you on its own.
Expect someone to say the two searches differ because one phrase is longer, so have the disjoint result ready. Zero records in common (C03), which a subset relationship can't produce.

Expect a second push on whether the comma is really the cause. Say what the deck says, that four cases fit and the mechanism is apparent rather than proven (C05, C06), and that the counts don't depend on it.
If anyone reads this as an accusation against Alaska Native corporations, point at slide 04 and slide 07, which say 8(a) is the mechanism Congress built and where the money goes when it comes home.
Note saves and comments at 48 hours against the last four decks, and write down whether the disjoint bracket on slide 02 or the four bar lengths on slide 05 were the frame people quoted back.
editor_notes_for_email:
Read slide 03 and slide 08 before posting. Slide 03 is the deck's argument and it is the one frame that is deliberately hedged on the page, because the comma mechanism is APPARENT, not proven, and the slide says so in its own guard line. If a reader takes that frame as a proven bug report the deck has overreached, so that guard line matters more than any other small type in the nine. Slide 08 is the counterweight and the frame most likely to be screenshotted out of context, since it sets an ICE task order beside the AI contracts; it is there because the same 8(a) mechanism buys both, and cutting it would make the deck a narrower and less honest thing. Slide 05's bars encode TIME and not dollars, which the slide states, and Koniag IT Systems' start is drawn hatched because the record does not carry one; a reader who measures the bars against the dollar figures printed beside them will find they disagree, and that is by design.

THREE THINGS THE PIXEL AND FLOW ROUNDS CHANGED that you should know about, because each was a real defect rather than a polish note.

First, slide 08 was printing an unsourced fact. The 102-signature Bering Straits line came from a scout note that the first claims pass never turned into a claim, so it reached a render with no claim-id behind it. It was verified during the pixel round against The Nome Nugget of January 8th, 2026, and is now C54 and C55. Verifying it also corrected it three ways. The 102 are shareholders AND descendants, it is an early-December count, and it excludes 20 non-shareholder signatures. The slide now prints all three qualifiers.

Second, slide 08's threshold paragraph said "This one is $632,119.41 above that line", and "this one" had no antecedent on that frame. The only contract named there is the ICE task order at $17,456,917.40, which is BELOW the $20 million line, so the sentence as built said the opposite of the record. It now names the Leisnoi contract. The same paragraph now opens "A law firm briefing reports that", because C42 is non-primary and no Pentagon document was reachable.

Third, a single line of drawing code was flattening EIGHT of the nine frames. The atmospheric limb glow was a radial gradient with an inner radius of S-6, and canvas fills everything inside that radius with the gradient's first stop, so a rim light was being added FLAT over the whole globe in additive mode. That was quietly erasing the grazing terminator the entire deck is built on. It is now a true annulus, which is why the frames read lit rather than washed. Seven were repaired in the pixel rounds by matching the text S-6; the eighth was written S-8, survived five more rounds, and was found only in Phase 12 by a new gate that MEASURES gradients instead of matching their names. That eighth frame is slide 07, and repairing it is what moved artwork craft from 7 to 8 and the deck from 8.78 to 9.07.

Also changed. Slide 09 lost the sentence "The federal fiscal year ends September 30th", because it carried no claim-id and claims.json has none for it. Slide 07 lost two rows and gained a KMXT attribution, because three non-primary background figures were being stated in the deck's own voice. Nothing in the locked caption reads as a factual error against claims.json, and the Johnston quote on slide 08 matches C43 word for word.

ONE COLLECTOR IS DOWN AND IT IS NOT THIS RUN'S. ledger/watch.json records a FAILED BASIS sweep, HTTP 503, with zero bills and zero hearings recorded against that failure. An empty queue after a failed sweep looks exactly like a quiet day, which is why it is written here rather than left to be inferred. The docket watch runs on its own workflow and not as a routine phase, so this run read it and did not write it.
